NEW PATIENT — establish care

23M, just started the EE PhD program, moved up for school. Last primary care was the college health service; asked them for his shot record. Wants a local doctor for physicals and for the blood work his psychiatrist needs.

Psych: bipolar I, diagnosed in college. Followed by an outside psychiatry group. Stable on lithium 300 twice a day and lamotrigine 100 daily, both prescribed by psychiatry. He says he is doing well, sleeping fine, no recent mood episodes he wants to talk about. Psychiatry would like lithium level, kidney and thyroid checks every 6 months and is fine with us drawing them.

PMH otherwise none. PSH none.
Meds: as above. No OTCs. Told him to avoid ibuprofen/naproxen and to keep hydrated in the heat while on lithium.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: father has bipolar I. Mother treated for depression. Mom's brother is "odd" per pt, never diagnosed with anything, pt says the family calls it schizotypal traits. Two siblings have cystic fibrosis. He says osteoporosis and stroke run in the family but isn't sure on whose side.
Social: grad student, lives with a roommate in Northampton. Never smoked. Drinks maybe once or twice a month, 1-2 drinks. No drugs.

ROS negative.

Exam: well appearing, pleasant, a little quiet. HEENT normal, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft. No tremor at rest or with arms extended. Skin normal. Mood "fine," affect a bit flat but reactive, thought process linear.

PHQ-9 3.

A/P
1. Bipolar I disorder — stable per pt, managed by psychiatry. Lithium level, BMP, TSH, CBC today. Will fax results to psychiatry. Recheck in ~6 months.
2. Health maintenance — Tdap today (last one was age 11 per pt, records pending). Lipids, HIV and hep C screening today. Flu shot when the vaccine comes in next month.
3. FHx CF in two siblings — noted; he has not had carrier testing. Not planning children right now.

RTC 6 mo for labs, 1 yr physical.

24M. Masked visit. Semester going remote mostly, he's been working in the lab on a reduced schedule.

Mood: no highs or lows he has noticed. Sleeping 7 hours. Taking lithium and lamotrigine every day, no missed doses that he can recall. Sees psychiatry by video every couple of months.

Today he brought up something he says has bothered him for years: he is uncomfortable around people, especially anyone who tries to get close, and has always been more comfortable on his own. Describes himself as a loner. He says he notices things in situations other people don't seem to notice. Not distressed in a crisis way, but he wants to understand it better. Not depressed. No SI.

He asked if this is part of the bipolar. Told him I don't know, and that his psychiatry group is the right place for a real diagnostic evaluation. He'd like a referral — his own psychiatrist mostly does med checks, and they have someone who does fuller evaluations.

Meds: lithium 300 BID, lamotrigine 100 daily. NKDA.
Social: unchanged. Never smoker, rare alcohol.

Exam: NAD. Avoids eye contact much of the visit. HEENT normal, thyroid not enlarged. Heart RRR no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft nontender. No tremor. Skin normal.
PHQ-9 4.

1. Bipolar I — stable. Lithium level, BMP, TSH, CBC today, results to psychiatry.
2. Long-standing interpersonal discomfort — referral to his psychiatry group for diagnostic evaluation.
3. HM — flu shot when it arrives, he'll come for a nurse visit. Tdap up to date (2019).

documents.title: Outpatient Psychiatry — Diagnostic Evaluation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY
Diagnostic evaluation, date of service 10/12/2020
Referred by: primary care

Thank you for sending Mr. Mercier for a fuller evaluation. He is known to our group for bipolar I disorder, managed with lithium and lamotrigine.

Reason for referral: lifelong unease in social settings and with closeness.

History: He tells me he has always been most comfortable alone and that relationships beyond a few people feel uncomfortable rather than rewarding. He experiences ordinary situations in an idiosyncratic way. He describes being able to feel what he calls the energy of the universe, and he endorses beliefs in clairvoyance and telepathy. He reports that now and then he thinks he hears his name spoken when nobody is nearby; this is brief, he doubts it afterward, and it does not have the quality of a voice talking to him. No sustained voices, no visual phenomena. No current manic or depressive symptoms; sleep regular.

Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 100 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: father with bipolar I; mother with major depression; a maternal uncle with schizotypal features, never formally diagnosed.
Social: EE graduate student, lives with a roommate. Never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks a month; no drugs.

Mental status: anxious. Speech somewhat odd in its phrasing and over-elaborate. Eye contact poor. Dress unusual and ornate for the setting. Thought process coherent and goal directed. Magical beliefs as above, held with some flexibility; no fixed delusions, no hallucinations in the formal sense. Insight partial. Judgment fair. Denies SI/HI.

Studies: CBC and thyroid function within normal limits; urine toxicology negative.

Impression: Schizotypal personality disorder, in a patient with bipolar I disorder that is currently euthymic. The perceptual experiences and odd beliefs are long-standing and occur outside mood episodes.

Plan:
- No medication change. Continue lithium 300 mg BID and lamotrigine 100 mg daily.
- No medication is indicated for the schizotypal features. Offered individual psychotherapy in our group, supportive and skills focused, to work on social comfort and on checking odd interpretations. He accepted; first session being scheduled.
- Continue med management visits every 2-3 months. Appreciate the semiannual lithium monitoring labs.

Outpatient psychiatry

documents.author: obstetrics and gynecology
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY
Preconception counseling, visit of 04/08/2022
Copy to primary care at the patient's request

Mr. Mercier was seen together with his partner, who is a patient of our practice, to talk about planning a pregnancy.

Relevant history: Two of his siblings have cystic fibrosis. He himself is well, with no history of lung, sinus or digestive problems and no findings on history or exam to suggest CF. He has never had CFTR testing, so whether he carries a variant is not known. His partner's family has no known history of CF.

Other history: bipolar I disorder and schizotypal personality disorder, followed by psychiatry. Medications lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 100 mg daily. No known drug allergies. Never smoker; drinks rarely.

Counseling: We reviewed that CF is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern through variants in the CFTR gene, so a child is affected only when both parents pass on a variant. Having two affected siblings and being unaffected himself raises his own chance of being a carrier well above the general population, where about 1 in 25 people carry a variant. We discussed carrier screening for both partners before conception and what each result would mean, including options if both were found to be carriers. The couple will think about testing and let us know.

Obstetrics & Gynecology

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Date of service: 10/21/2025
(received with inpatient records)

Chief complaint: roommate concerned about worsening behavior for 10 days.

HPI: 30-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and schizotypal personality disorder, maintained on lithium and lamotrigine, seen here three years ago for a similar presentation that led to admission. Per roommate, over the past week and a half he has been getting one to two hours of sleep a night, talking almost without pause, changing subjects abruptly, and making large impulsive purchases online. He tells us he has built a device that lets him talk with satellites. He believes government agents are following him by tracking his phone.

Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 100 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: father bipolar I disorder, mother major depressive disorder, maternal uncle with undiagnosed schizotypal traits.
Social: electrical engineering graduate student; never smoker; occasional alcohol, 1-2 drinks a month.

Exam: restless, unable to sit for long. Speech fast and pressured, thoughts tangential. Irritable but cooperative. Oriented to person, place and time. Otherwise medically unremarkable.

Labs: urine toxicology negative.

Assessment: acute manic episode with psychotic features, bipolar I disorder. Not intoxicated.

documents.title: Inpatient Psychiatry Discharge Summary
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
INPATIENT PSYCHIATRY — DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 10/21/2025 from the ED. Discharged 10/28/2025.

Admitting diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with psychotic features.
Other: schizotypal personality disorder.

Course: On arrival to the unit he remained pressured, grandiose and disorganized; overnight staff found him trying to give lectures to other patients about how to unlock the secrets of the universe. For the first days his speech stayed rapid, his mood elevated, and the beliefs about his satellite device and being tracked were unchanged. Lithium and lamotrigine were continued at home doses and olanzapine 10 mg at bedtime was added. By about day 5 his sleep had lengthened, his mood was coming down and his thinking was more organized. At discharge he was calm, linear, sleeping 6-7 hours, no longer voicing the tracking beliefs, and future oriented. No safety concerns during the stay.

Discharge medications:
- Lithium carbonate 300 mg by mouth twice daily (continued)
- Lamotrigine 100 mg by mouth daily (continued)
- Haloperidol 5 mg by mouth daily (NEW)
Olanzapine was used during the stay and is not continued.

Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: outpatient psychiatry within one week; PCP as scheduled.
Condition at discharge: improved, stable.

Inpatient psychiatry

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Date of service: 10/28/2025, arrival 19:25
Copy to PCP

Chief complaint: neck pain, tight face, can't control eyes.

HPI: 30-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and schizotypal personality disorder, brought by his roommate. He was discharged from our inpatient psychiatric unit this morning after a week-long admission for mania with psychotic features (pressured speech, grandiosity, disorganized behavior). A new medication was started at discharge to stabilize mood and prevent relapse; the roommate confirms it is haloperidol, a high-potency antipsychotic. He took the first dose at home around 13:00. About five hours later he felt an odd pulling in his jaw and stiffness at the back of his neck. Over the following hour the pain worsened and his eyes rolled upward on their own. He could not bring his head back to midline and became very distressed, so the roommate drove him in. He has never had anything like this before. He had not taken an antipsychotic before this hospitalization. No alcohol or drugs recently. No head injury.
ROS: no fever, no confusion, no generalized stiffness, no tremor.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID, lamotrigine 100 mg daily, haloperidol 5 mg daily (one dose taken).
Allergies: NKDA on arrival.
Family: father bipolar I; mother major depressive disorder; maternal uncle with schizotypal traits.
Social: EE graduate student. Nonsmoker. Occasional alcohol. No substance use history.

Vitals: T 37.0 C (98.6 F), HR 82, RR 14, BP 124/78.

Exam: awake, alert, oriented x3, anxious and sweaty. Head held tilted to one side, jaw partly clenched. Eyes fixed in upward gaze. Heart and lungs normal. Sustained contraction of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Strength and sensation intact, no focal deficit. Limbs without rigidity; no tremor; no cogwheeling.

Labs: BMP within normal limits. CK 165 U/L. Lithium 0.7 mmol/L.

ED course: Benztropine 2 mg IV given at 20:10. Within about 20 minutes the eye deviation and neck spasm released and he could move his head and eyes normally. Observed for 3 hours without recurrence. No fever or rigidity to suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome; CK normal.

Impression: Oculogyric crisis / acute dystonic reaction to haloperidol, first dose.

Plan:
- Stop haloperidol. Do not restart. Haloperidol added to allergy/intolerance list (acute dystonia).
- Benztropine 1 mg by mouth twice daily for 3 days.
- Continue lithium and lamotrigine.
- Inpatient psychiatry team notified; outpatient psychiatry to call him tomorrow about an alternative.
- Return for any recurrence, fever, confusion or stiffness.
Disposition: discharged home with roommate 23:40.

documents.title: ED and Hospital Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/U after psych admission and ED visit.

He missed his 10/16 appt here — turns out he was already getting sick then. Admitted to inpatient psych 10/21-10/28 at outside hospital for mania with psychotic features (second time in 3 years). Discharge summary not received yet; ED record from 10/28 reviewed. Discharged on haloperidol in addition to his lithium/lamotrigine, and that evening after the first dose developed an oculogyric crisis — eyes up, neck pulled over. Benztropine IV in the ED fixed it. 3 days of oral benztropine, done Friday. No recurrence since.

Psychiatry called him the next day and put him back on olanzapine 10 mg at bedtime, which he had in the hospital without trouble. Pharmacy fill notices match. Psych appointment in two weeks.

Now: sleeping 8-9 h, "foggy" in the mornings, mood "normal-ish, maybe a little low." No racing thoughts. Says the satellite stuff "sounds crazy now." No SI. Partner and roommate checking in. Out of lab work for the rest of the month by agreement with his advisor.

Meds reconciled today: lithium 300 BID, lamotrigine 100 daily, olanzapine 10 qhs. Haloperidol off the list. Benztropine course complete.
Allergies updated: haloperidol — acute dystonia.

Exam: calm, slowed slightly, linear, appropriate. No abnormal movements, no torticollis, EOM full. No rigidity, no tremor. Heart and lungs normal.
PHQ-9 8.

A/P
1. Bipolar I disorder, recent manic episode with psychotic features — improving on lithium, lamotrigine, olanzapine. Psychiatry managing.
2. Oculogyric crisis from haloperidol — resolved. Avoid haloperidol.
3. Olanzapine — baseline metabolic monitoring: weight today 74 kg, A1c, fasting-ish lipids, CMP. Will repeat A1c in ~3 months and lipids/weight at the physical. Lithium 0.7 in the ED last week, no need to repeat today; TSH due.
4. Flu and COVID today.
